title: Skeletal muscle enhancer programming of intrinsic cardiorespiratory fitness
authors: Weitzel, A. M.; Orchard, P.; Evans, C.; Manickam, N.; Treutelaar, M. K.; Britton, S. L.; Koch, L. G.; Li, J. Z.; Parker, S. C. J.; Burant, C. F.
abstract: Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is a heritable trait associated with improved metabolic health and longevity. Integrating 546 transcriptomic and epigenomic profiles from skeletal muscle of 128 genetically heterogeneous rats selectively bred for high and low running capacity (HCR and LCR), a model that mirrors CRF-associated traits in humans, we identify a distributed enhancer architecture underlying their divergent transcriptomes. Line-divergent alleles were concentrated in distal enhancers: those more active in HCR were enriched for ETS-family transcription factor motifs and positively linked to hundreds of mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and angiogenesis genes, whereas those more active in LCR were enriched for Mef2 motifs and negatively linked to these genes. In 426 genotype, gene expression, and chromatin accessibility profiles from an independent HCRxLCR F2 population (n=147), we validated thousands of these genetic effects. Thus, heritable CRF reflects many enhancers cumulatively tuning energy metabolism and oxygen delivery, providing a molecular basis for variation in CRF.

title: Design of Orthogonal Far-Red, Orange and Green Fluorophore-binding Proteins for Multiplex Imaging
authors: Tran, L.; Klein, S.; Sharma, S.; Juergens, D.; Decarreau, J.; Liu, B.; Wang, Y.; Bera, A. K.; Kang, A.; Woods, J.; Joyce, E.; Vafeados, D. K.; Roullier, N.; Chen, W.; Lee, G. R.; Lavis, L. D.; Mahamid, J.; An, L.; Baker, D.
abstract: Fluorescent proteins have transformed biological imaging, yet their limited photostability and brightness restrict their applications. We used deep learning-based de novo protein design methods to design binders to three bright, stable and cell-permeable dyes spanning the imaging spectrum: JF657 (far red), JF596 (orange-red) and JF494 (green). We obtain highly specific dye-binding proteins with low nanomolar affinities for the intended target; a crystal structure of one binder confirms close resemblance to the design model. Simultaneous labeling of mammalian cells expressing three dye-specific binders at different subcellular compartments demonstrates the utility in multiplex imaging. We further expand the functionality of the binder by incorporating an active site that carries out nucleophilic aromatic substitution to form a covalent linkage with the dye, and develop split versions which reconstitute fluorescence at subcellular locations where both halves are present towards monitoring in-cell protein interactions and chemically induced dimerization. Our designed high affinity and specificity dye binders open up new opportunities for multiplexed biological imaging.

title: Structural features and conservation of the lncRNA HOTAIR in primates
authors: Perry, Z. R.; Beeram, A.; Lee, L.; Pyle, A. M.
abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate diverse cellular processes and are frequently implicated in disease, but their functional mechanisms often remain elusive. One such lncRNA, HOTAIR (Hox transcript antisense intergenic RNA), is a ~2.1 kb mammalian transcript whose overexpression promotes invasion and metastasis in breast cancer. However, the mechanisms by which HOTAIR influences gene regulation in cancer are poorly understood. To approach this problem through a structural lens, we predicted the full-length in cellulo secondary structure of HOTAIR using chemical probing in a metastatic breast cancer cell line. The resulting structure shows that HOTAIR adopts a multidomain architecture and has local structural features unique to the cellular context. Comparison between in vitro and in cellulo chemical probing identifies regions of differential accessibility that may indicate context-dependent molecular interactions or folding. Conservation analyses further reveal that HOTAIR is conserved across primates with evidence of structural covariation in specific domains. Together, these results provide a roadmap for future mechanistic studies of structure-function relationships in HOTAIR and its contribution to gene regulation in cancer.

title: Molecular sterics guide tmRNA translocation on the ribosome
authors: Wanes, G.; Keiler, K. C.; Dunham, C. M.; Whitford, P. C.
abstract: Translation of defective mRNA transcripts can lead to the formation of stalled ``non-stop'' ribosome complexes. To rescue these ribosomes, bacteria have evolved a mechanism called trans-translation that is mediated by transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA) and small protein B (SmpB). During the translocation step of trans-translation, the stalled mRNA is ejected and the reading frame found in the mRNA-like domain (MLD) of tmRNA is loaded into the mRNA channel. The ribosome then translates the new template, thereby tagging the nascent protein for degradation. While structures of tmRNA-SmpB on the ribosome have been available for years, little is known about the molecular factors that govern the dynamics of tmRNA translocation. Here, we use an energetically smooth model (i.e. SMOG) to simulate translocation of tmRNA-SmpB, which reveals that the structure of the ribosome gives rise to a preferred sequence of conformational substeps. Specifically, the tRNA-like domain (TLD) translocates, then the MLD loads, and finally the C-terminal tail of SmpB rearranges. These steps are interdependent and associated with a range of sterically-induced barriers that regulate the kinetics. This provides a structural and energetic framework for understanding, and ultimately controlling, the dynamics of trans-translation.

title: Amide I kurtosis maps cardiac amyloid in human tissue by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy
authors: Ota, K.; Chen, T.-H.; Yamaguchi, T.; Otsubo, T.; Murakami, Y.; Masaki, M.; Leproux, P.; Suzuki, R.; Node, K.; Kano, H.
abstract: Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposits of misfolded proteins in the heart and can lead to heart failure. Histological confirmation typically involves staining tissue sections with Congo red and examining them under polarized light for apple-green birefringence; however, achieving an interpretable, label-free, and observer-independent assessment remains challenging. Here we show that Pearson kurtosis of channel intensities within the amide I window provides an interpretable, fitting-free contrast for cardiac amyloid in unstained human cardiac tissue sections from ten participants imaged by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS). In a discovery participant, high-kurtosis regions corresponded with Congo red-positive tissue in two CARS-histology pairs of adjacent sections (descriptive spatial AUCs, 0.79 and 0.73). Across 15 fields from nine additional participants, field-level kurtosis values did not overlap between severe-deposition and Congo red-negative tissue fields. Among the descriptors examined, kurtosis showed the largest standardized participant-level separation. Exploratory multivariate curve resolution yielded a deposit-associated component with aromatic-residue features shared with reagent transthyretin. In one field from the discovery participant, the second harmonic generation (SHG) signal, acquired simultaneously with CARS, showed a broadly inverse spatial pattern relative to the amide I kurtosis map, revealing distinct tissue-architectural contrast. Together, these findings support a potential label-free approach to detecting cardiac amyloid deposits that combines amide I kurtosis derived from broadband CARS with SHG-derived architectural contrast.

title: Potassium modulates Phytophthora zoospore motility and flagellar beating through dose-dependent effects
authors: Lupatelli, C. A.; ATTARD, A.; Galiana, E.; Cohen, C.; Thomen, P.; Noblin, X.
abstract: Biflagellate zoospores are critical agents in the spread of Phytophthora spp., plant pathogens causing major agronomic and economic losses worldwide. These motile cells navigate soil water films toward plant roots using taxis triggered by environmental cues. Here, we investigate how potassium modulates zoospore motility by analyzing trajectory and flagellar beating parameters across KCl concentrations. Using high-speed imaging, we apply kymograph analysis and Fourier transform of the cell body direction over time to quantify flagellar dynamics, while low-speed imaging provides trajectory characteristics. Our results demonstrate that increasing potassium concentration significantly reduces swimming speed while enhancing directional changes. We establish a direct correlation between altered swimming speed and changes in flagellar beating parameters. Our findings indicate that potassium differentially affects anterior and posterior flagella beating. Furthermore, potassium exerts multiple effects, influencing beat amplitude, wave propagation speed and direction- change frequency. This reveals potassium as a key modulator of zoospore motility, triggering a shift from exploratory swimming to confined, reoriented movement. By uncovering the biomechanical responses of zoospores to potassium, this study advances our understanding of how surrounding signals regulate pathogen dispersal in the environment.

title: STRUCTURAL AND MOLECULAR DYNAMICS ANALYSIS OF HUMAN β-DEFENSIN 1 VARIANTS REVEALS DISTINCT PERTURBATION SIGNATURES
authors: Fogarty, R. J.; Urrutia, R.; Pinto e Vairo, F.; Hong, J. C.; Lomberk, G.
abstract: Human {beta}-defensin 1 (hBD-1) is a small, disulfide-constrained antimicrobial peptide produced predominantly in the kidney and urogenital tract, where it contributes to epithelial innate defense. Genetic variation in the gene encoding hBD-1 has been associated with altered expression levels and susceptibility to infections, including infection following solid organ transplantation, yet the molecular consequences of coding substitutions in the active, mature form remain largely undefined. Here, we integrate conventional genomics, protein bioinformatics, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics to investigate the molecular consequences of 93 human-observed hBD-1 missense variants. Evaluation of hBD-1 missense variants across sequence-, structure-, and dynamics-based dimensions reveals variant-specific molecular perturbation signatures that complement conventional and static biophysical predictions. By treating naturally occurring substitutions as a perturbation series across a compact defensin scaffold, this study identifies multiple molecular routes through which sequence variation can remodel an endogenous antimicrobial peptide and prioritizes variants for direct structure-function testing. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for investigating how naturally occurring hBD-1 variation may influence peptide behavior and, ultimately, antimicrobial function.

title: Cross-linker binding strength influences actin assembly microstructure and myosin II driven remodeling
authors: Feigeles, C. A.; Janquart, M.; Armstrong, V.; Weirich, K. L.
abstract: The actin cytoskeleton is a self-assembled material that acts as the mechanical scaffold of the cell. Within the cell, protein cross-linkers organize actin filaments into assemblies with various microstructures that support distinct physiological functions. These protein cross-linkers differ in structural features. To decouple the role of individual cross-linker properties in actin assembly microstructure and mechanics, we synthesize programmable cross-linkers using a DNA linker coupled to binding domains. We find that high affinity cross-linkers induce actin bundling, while low affinity cross-linkers form actin networks. Myosin II motors remodel and contract all cross-linked networks tested in distinct ways from uncross-linked networks. We find that networks with high affinity cross-linkers have different myosin induced dynamics than networks with low affinity cross-linkers. This research expands our understanding of how cells regulate their mechanics and microstructures, while also providing insight towards the structure-property relationship in complex soft materials.

title: Synthesis and characterization of NIR fluorescent BODIPY-Xanthene hybrid dyes
authors: Nigianni, G.; Katsamakas, S.; Alexandratou, E.; Prousis, K. C.
abstract: The development of NIR fluorescent dyes with favorable optical properties is of great importance especially for applications within the field of optical imaging. In this study, we report the design, synthesis and photophysical characterization of novel BODIPY-Xanthene hybrid dyes obtained via Knoevenagel condensation between an asymmetrical BODIPY core and the functionalized xanthene aldehydes intermediates. The synthesized dyes ex-hibit absorption (667 nm) and emission bands (720-722 nm) within the NIR region. Detailed UV-Vis and fluo-rescence studies were performed and molar extinction coefficients and stokes shifts also calculated. Moreover, findings highlighting the influence of structural modifications on the optical behavior of the hybrid dyes and their potential utility in optical imaging applications are reported.

title: Quantification of cellular contributions to multi-cellular pattern formation
authors: Estavoyer, M.; Zhao, M. L.; Merkel, M.
abstract: Multi-cellular pattern formation is a key process in organism development, regeneration, and disease. Such multi-cellular patterns include, for instance, cell density and gene expression patterns. Here, we develop a cell-track-based method that quantifies how much individual cellular processes contribute to the emergence of large-scale patterns. These cellular processes include changes in cellular expression levels, cell motion, cell divisions, and apoptosis. We validate our method using synthetic data, before demonstrating it on two sets of experimental data. Our method is purely geometric and does not require any mechanistic assumptions about the underlying pattern-forming processes, making it very generic and robust. It thus enables unbiased, data-driven study of the mechanisms driving pattern formation across a broad class of systems.

title: Microscopic collisions govern macroscopic aerotactic spreading through emergent transport coefficients
authors: Ghazi, N.; Hirose, S.; Funamoto, K.; Calvez, V.; Anjard, C.; Cochet-Escartin, O.; Demircigil, M.; RIEU, J.-P.
abstract: Collective migration is often attributed to complex cell-cell communication, yet coordinated multicellular dynamics can also emerge in organisms lacking social interactions. Continuum descriptions successfully capture such behaviors but generally rely on phenomenological transport coefficients whose microscopic origin remains elusive. Here we show that these coefficients emerge from cell-cell collisions and can be independently determined from experiments. We investigate the aerotactic dispersal of confined colonies of the solitary amoeba Acanthamoeba castellanii, in which oxygen consumption continuously reshapes the local environment to generate self-organized guidance cues. Combining quantitative videomicroscopy, oxygen mapping with phosphorescent sensing films, and oxygen-controlled microfluidics, we directly measure both the oxygen landscape and the aerotactic response governing colony expansion. We then develop a Patlak-Keller-Segel (PKS) -type drift-diffusion model whose transport coefficients are entirely determined from independent experiments and microscopic-to-macroscopic modeling approach, without adjustable parameters. The model quantitatively reproduces the observed dynamics, including the coexistence of a fast ballistic front and a trailing transient accumulation band. We show that both diffusion and aerotactic transport are modulated by the same collision-controlled mechanism through density-dependent changes in cell persistence. More generally, our results establish transport coefficients as measurable emergent properties bridging microscopic cell dynamics and macroscopic collective behavior, providing a predictive framework for oxygen-guided migration in living active matter.

title: A deep learning-generated hASIC1a miniprotein inhibitor confers neuroprotection in stroke
authors: Sormann, J.; Epitropaki, K.; Vicino, M. F.; Fjorbak, C. L.; Pugh, C. F.; Lang, B.; Beyer, E. K.; Comaposada-Baro, R.; Hink, F.; Friis, S.; Usher, S. G.; Cai, C.; Autzen, H. E.; Rogers, J. M.; Pless, S.
abstract: Ion channels remain notoriously recalcitrant drug targets despite their extensive pathophysiological significance. Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are proton-gated cation channels that cause neuronal death when excessively activated, such as during ischaemic stroke. This acidosis-driven injury pathway remains unchallenged by existing therapeutics. Here we generate two de novo designed hASIC1a-specific miniproteins by developing a platform that integrates computational miniprotein design, high-throughput automated patch clamp screening, biophysical and structural characterisation, and in vivo validation. We identify a subtype-selective hASIC1a inhibitor, Denasin1, which achieves near-complete inhibition with nanomolar potency. Denasin1 is disordered in solution but adopts the computationally predicted helix-turn-helix fold when bound to the extracellular acidic pocket of hASIC1a. Crucially, Denasin1 reduces infarct volume by > 50% in a murine model of ischaemic stroke. We thereby establish our de novo design platform as a route to develop potent and selective ion channel modulators.

title: Structural Insights into the Expanded Substrate Scope of a Cysteine-Dependent Hydrolase from Rhodococcus opacus for Polyethylene, Polypropylene, and Polystyrene Biodegradation
authors: Aggarwal, S.; Singh, S.; Kayastha, A.; Aggarwal, D.; Jangid, K.; Shakib, M.; Singh, D.; Sharma, A. K.; Kumar, P.
abstract: Microplastic pollution from homopolymers such as polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and polyethylene (PE) poses growing health and environmental concerns, highlighting the need for robust polymer-degrading biocatalysts. We previously identified a naturally occurring cysteine-dependent hydrolase (CsdH) from Rhodococcus opacus, featuring a unique Cys160-Lys127-Asp39 catalytic triad and providing a novel mechanism for polyethylene terephthalate (PET) degradation. In this study, we have determined crystal structures of CsdH in complex with PP, PS, PE, and styrene and demonstrated the potential of the enzyme to directly degrade these homopolymers into their respective low molecular weight degradation products using LC-MS. Structural analysis reveals that the enzyme retains a conserved principal access tunnel while undergoing subtle substrate-dependent changes to accommodate different substrates. The enzyme exhibited broad plastic degradation activity with the highest weight loss observed for PE, followed by PP and PS. SEM analysis reveals surface roughness, cracks and grooves, confirming polymer degradation. Further, these results corroborate through FTIR and TGA analysis. These findings establish a strong foundation for enzyme engineering and aim at developing efficient microplastic degradation.

title: A transient third metal ion shapes the catalytic cycle of a group I intron ribozyme
authors: McCarthy, E.; Ekesan, S.; Giese, T. J.; Du, Y.; Barletta, G. P.; Götz, A. W.; Piccirilli, J. A.; York, D. M.
abstract: The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of biochemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between Gexo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5' exon splice site nucleotide, U(-1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the Gexo in the first step, and analogously the G{omega} in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the pKa at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(-1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications.

title: Physical Basis Of pKa Shift For Ionizable Lipids In An LNP-like Environment
authors: Sharma, A.; Sur, S.; Grossfield, A.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading drug delivery platform for mRNA or other nucleic acid-based therapeutics. LNP platforms are typically composed of ionizable aminolipids, phospholipids, sterols, and lipids tagged with polyethylene glycol. The ionizable aminolipids are typically cationic at low pH, allowing them to encapsulate negatively charged mRNA. The pH at which the ionizable head groups change charge states, the apparent pKa, is crucial to understand the characteristics and formulation of LNP. However, this is difficult to measure as the apparent pKa differs from the pKa of the aminolipids in bulk solution due to the complex chemical and charge environment. In this study, we use molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with alchemical free energy perturbation to calculate the pKa shift as a function of lipid composition, treating LNP-like and vesicle-like environments. Our results show that the pH-dependent structure of the systems affects the trends in pKa shifts in complex ways, driven by factors including surface electrostatics and lipid internalization. Our all-atom simulation protocol allows us to efficiently estimate the apparent pKa of LNP-like models formed with novel ionizable aminolipids and estimate how it will change with composition.

title: Crowding governs resistance confinement and guides the improvement of adaptive therapy in a 2D melanoma model system
authors: Kayser, J.; Eiche, M.; Fischer, E. F.; Smith, A.-S.; Milas, M.; Citak, T.; Aif, S.
abstract: The emergence of treatment resistant mutants is one of the primary contributors to therapy failure in cancer. Evolution-based adaptive therapies aim to exploit the competition between sensitive and resistant cells to prolong therapeutic control. However, in the densely packed tissues of solid tumors, competition is not only determined by cell-intrinsic factors but also a result of local physical interactions between neighboring cells. The successful development of physics-informed adaptive therapies therefore hinges upon the bottom-up integration of tissue mechanics and experimentally grounded models of tumor evolution. Here, we show how population-level treatment response emerges from mechanical interactions between individual cells. Combining genetically tailored therapy-mimicry experiments in spatially structured 2D melanoma colonies with mechanistic, particle-based tissue simulations as digital twins in a real-to-sim-to-real framework, we reveal how treatment-induced changes in mechanical crowding shape a cascade of resistance expansion, spatial competitive escape, and consequent therapy failure. We then link these underlying physical mechanisms to population-level observables in an abstracted mathematical model for reinforcement-learning-based therapy optimization and a distilled treatment-decision-heuristic, which we test experimentally. Together, our results identify mechanical crowding and escape as governing principles of resistance-mediated therapy failure in solid tumours and provide a basis for mechanistically informed, evolution-based treatment strategies.

title: Grow2Fold: mapping heterogeneous developmental growth to human brain folding
authors: Hou, J.; Solhtalab, A.; Jiang, K.; Gu, B.; Li, T.; Chen, X.; Wu, T.; Song, K.; Liu, Y.; Song, W.; zhu, D.; Liu, T.; Kuhl, E.; Li, G.; Razavi, M. J.; Wang, X.
abstract: Cortical folding emerges through complex developmental processes, yet what organizes these processes into the characteristic folding patterns of the human brain remains unclear. Here, we developed an imaging-informed whole-brain modeling framework, Grow2Fold, that integrates developmental cortical regionalization, quantitative growth characterization, and mechanics-guided simulation to investigate how cortical growth shapes brain folding patterns. Using 836 fetal and neonatal MRI sessions from 747 participants spanning 21-45 postmenstrual weeks, we identified a reproducible and hierarchical spatiotemporal organization of cortical expansion characterized by coordinated regional growth trajectories. Rapid expansion occurs earlier around peri-central territories and progressively shifts toward frontal, parietal, and temporal association cortices. We encoded these imaging-derived trajectories into region- and age-specific growth laws and incorporated them into anatomically realistic whole-brain mechanical models. The resulting simulations recapitulate major sulcal landmarks and characteristic folding development across global and regional morphological measures. Comparing regional and uniform growth, we find that differential growth drives cortical instability, while heterogeneous developmental growth organizes this instability into anatomically recognizable folding patterns. Combined with subject-specific anatomy, these population-informed growth laws reproduce individualized longitudinal folding trajectories. Together, our results identify spatiotemporally patterned developmental growth as a key spatial constraint on cortical morphogenesis and establish a quantitative bridge from developmental imaging, through mechanical instability, to anatomically organized folding.

title: CryoFAST: A Fab-Aided Cryo-EM Workflow for High-Resolution Structure Determination of Sub-50-kDa Protein Targets
authors: Li, X.; Deng, S.; Li, W.; Qian, Y.; Li, Y.; Du, J.; Li, L.; Qian, D.
abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) plays an increasingly important role in structure-based drug discovery (SBDD) by revealing target protein-ligand interactions at the molecular level, but its application has largely focused on large- and medium-sized protein complexes. Many therapeutically important targets are smaller than 50 kDa and remain highly challenging for cryo-EM analysis because of low signal-to-noise ratios and difficulties in particle alignment. Here, we describe cryoFAST, an integrated workflow that couples ligand-compatible Fab discovery and structure-guided computational maturation with biochemical triage, fiducial-complex assembly, and single-particle cryo-EM. Through phage-display screening and/or AI-guided design, we developed high-affinity Fab binders of approximately 50 kDa that stabilize the target without disrupting ligand-target interactions and then assembled Fab-target complexes for cryo-EM analysis. Using the therapeutically relevant extracellular domain (~20 kDa) of interleukin-4 receptor (IL-4R) as a proof of concept, we determined its cryo-EM structure at 2.74 Angstrom resolution and established a framework for elucidating ligand-binding modes. This workflow provides a practical, efficient, and potentially broadly applicable route to the structural characterization of small protein targets that are otherwise challenging to study. By extending the applicability of cryo-EM to high-value but technically challenging small targets, cryoFAST may open new opportunities for structure-based drug discovery.

title: Structural Basis for Near Infrared Absorption and Noncanonical Photoisomerization in Neorhodopsin
authors: Kovalev, K.; Boehlke, B.; Nag, P.; Grosse, M.; Kraskov, A.; Katz, S.; Hildebrandt, P.; Bartl, F.; Schapiro, I.; Hegemann, P.; Broser, M.
abstract: In retinal proteins, light absorption leads to a double bond isomerization of the chromophore, followed by conformational relaxations that drive functional protein rearrangements. The balance between photoisomerization and radiative or non-radiative decays of the excited state is adjusted to the demands of the respective photoreceptor function. The molecular determinants controlling the excited state processes remain poorly understood and are the focus of this combined crystallographic, spectroscopic, and theoretical work on the recently discovered neorhodopsin (NeoR). NeoR exhibits a highly red-shifted and fluorescent dark state and selectively photoisomerizes from all-trans to 7-cis. We show that the local electrostatic environment reduces the negative charge density near the Schiff base and suppresses torsional motion around the canonical C13=C14 isomerization site of microbial rhodopsins. Instead, the chromophore-binding pocket permits only low-efficiency C7=C8 isomerization, accompanied by polyene inversion, {beta}-ionone ring displacement, and Schiff base deprotonation. Consequently, unlike other retinal photoreceptors, NeoR undergoes structural changes localized near the {beta}-ionone ring.

title: An AI-Enabled Translational Drug Discovery Framework for NALCN Channelopathy: From High-Throughput Screening to Therapeutic Candidate
authors: Thongsepee, N.; Tanner, J. A.; Polusani, S.; Typou, A.; Clanton, N. A.; Holmes, B. B.; Lory, P.; Dwyer, D. S.; Zhou, D.; Monteil, A.; Yuan, Y.
abstract: Background: More than 90% of rare diseases lack an approved therapy, partly reflecting economic barriers in developing treatments for small patient populations. A common bottleneck is costly and resource-intensive hit-to-lead prioritization. Congenital contractures of the limbs and face, hypotonia, and developmental delay (CLIFAHDD) is an ultra-rare neurodevelopmental disease often caused by de novo gain-of-function variants in the sodium leak channel NALCN, with no approved treatments. Methods: We developed a cost and resource-efficient, AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic high-throughput screening (HTS), structural biology foundation models for hit-to-lead prioritization, and orthogonal experimental validation. We applied this framework for drug repurposing to identify NALCN inhibitors as therapeutic candidates for CLIFAHDD. We screened ~1,200 approved drugs using a fluorescence-based membrane potential assay in doxycycline-inducible HEK293 cells stably expressing the NALCN channelosome. Boltz-2 modeling predicted binding affinity and mode to prioritize hits. Lead repurposing candidates were selected by a multidisciplinary expert review panel. Lead candidates were evaluated using patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells expressing wild-type or CLIFAHDD-associated NALCN variants, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and a C. elegans NALCN gain-of-function model. Results: HTS identified 11 candidate NALCN inhibitors. Boltz-2 prioritized candidates based on predicted binding affinity and predicted binding within the NALCN pore, consistent with a direct pore-blocking mechanism. Aprepitant emerged as the lead candidate after multidisciplinary evaluation based on its predicted mechanism, pharmacologic properties, blood-brain barrier penetration, established safety profile, and regulatory approval in children and adults. Patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed partial inhibition of NALCN-mediated sodium leak currents in HEK293 cells (IC50;=2.22 M), with comparable potency against Cav3.1 (IC50=1.63 M). In primary mouse hippocampal neurons, aprepitant reduced sodium leak currents, hyperpolarized resting membrane potential, and decreased spontaneous firing. Aprepitant rescued hyperlocomotor and dystonic phenotypes in a C. elegans gain-of-function NALCN model. There was notable concordance between AI-predicted hits, phenotypic screening hits, and experimental validation. Conclusion: These findings identify aprepitant as a lead therapeutic candidate for CLIFAHDD, and establish an AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic screening, structural modeling, and experimental validation for NALCN channelopathies. This scalable and resource-conscious strategy may accelerate hit-to-lead prioritization and drug discovery for rare and ultra-rare diseases lacking effective therapies.

title: Mechanistic simulation identifies predictive dose-dependent biomarkers of propofol anesthesia
authors: Pathak, A.; Brincat, S. L.; Xiong, Y.; Organtzidis, H.; Protter, M.; Du, V.; Strey, H. H.; Mujica-Parodi, L. R.; Miller, E. K.; Granger, R.
abstract: Understanding how receptor-level modulation reorganizes large-scale brain circuits remains a central challenge in neuropharmacology. Here we introduce a multiscale mechanistic model with explicit core-matrix thalamocortical architecture to examine how propofol reorganizes brainwide activity from individual receptors to systems-level circuits. Crucially, the model did not involve machine learning or statistical fitting to pre-existing anesthesia data. We use the model to simulate the multi-scale effects of propofol, which range from modulation of individual synaptic conductances to widespread alterations of neural spiking, field potentials, and coherence. Without requiring any training on task-specific data, our simulation of sensory processing in a standard auditory oddball paradigm matches independent data from anesthetized and awake behaving macaques. The same simulation, unmodified, also reproduces changes to functional connectivity in anesthetized humans, exhibiting selective attenuation of matrix thalamocortical loops relative to core loops. Most importantly, the simulation identified a previously unknown biomarker of propofol concentration: elevated residual inter-stimulus cortical activity. This dose-dependent biomarker was subsequently confirmed in empirical macaque data, where it had previously gone unnoticed. This simulation-first discovery, arising from mechanistic circuit dynamics rather than statistical comparison of clinical populations, serves as an illustrative example of a broader generative framework that can translate receptor-level modulation into circuit-scale biomarkers with potential applications across predictive neuropharmacology.

title: Robust brain inspired prediction of speech recognition accuracy across many words, voices, and natural background sounds
authors: Clonan, A. C.; Stevenson, I. H.; Escabi, M. A.
abstract: Although humans generally excel at recognizing speech in noisy natural environments, performance varies widely due to differences in the background acoustics and individual talker attributes such as voice quality, intonation, and pitch. The underlying neural and acoustic factors of this perceptual variability remain elusive, making it an unresolved challenge to predict when speech recognition will succeed or fail. Here, we characterize human speech recognition across a wide range of natural conditions using speech spoken by 326 diverse male and female talkers of multiple ages embedded in 33 unique background noises. Across this vast soundscape, speech recognition is strongly driven by the spectrum and modulation statistics of the noise. Yet, articulatory speech features - including fundamental and formant frequencies - exert categorically distinct modulatory effects on recognition accuracy across the talkers age and gender, and specific words. This perceptual variability is captured by a low-dimensional statistical representation of sounds based on computations that emulate intermediate stages of sound processing and feature extraction in auditory midbrain. A model utilizing these sound summary statistics accurately predicts individual listeners single-trial recognition behavior, accounting for performance variance across individual voices, words, and backgrounds. Thus, speech-in-noise perception across diverse natural conditions relies largely on a simple set of spectrotemporal summary statistics known to be represented by central neural populations. Significance StatementAlthough humans can easily maintain conversations amidst environmental noise and voice variations, this capacity is severely degraded by hearing impairment and challenges modern speech recognition technologies. This study evaluates human speech recognition across a broad spectrum of environmental noises and diverse speaker demographics. We show that a brain-inspired auditory representation of sounds extracts critical statistical sound features driving human behavior, precisely predicting variations in perceptual accuracy across distinct voices, words, and environmental backgrounds.

title: An ancestral tRNA maturation enzyme repurposed for cytoplasmic non-coding RNA processing
authors: Shaukat, A.-N.; Dondeti, M. F.; Maniatis, A.; Skeparnias, I.; Kaliatsi, E. G.; Anastasakis, D. G.; Zhang, J.; Vourekas, A.; Stathopoulos, C.
abstract: Ribonuclease Z enzymes remove 3' trailers from precursor tRNAs. In human cells, ELAC2/RNase ZL matures nuclear and mitochondrial pre-tRNAs, whereas the cytosolic short paralog ELAC1/RNase ZS repairs ANKZF1-cleaved tRNAs, but its broader substrate repertoire remains unclear. We investigated ELAC1 function using transcriptome profiling, small RNA sequencing, CLIP-seq, and biochemical reconstitution. ELAC1 was dispensable for canonical tRNA processing but associated with structured RNA polymerase III transcripts, prominently Y RNAs and vault RNAs (vtRNAs). Purified ELAC1 cleaved all four human vtRNAs near their 3' ends, with high-resolution mapping identifying a conserved cleavage position within the 3' extension. Efficient cleavage required structural features of the vtRNA terminal region. In contrast, ELAC2 showed little or no vtRNA cleavage under the conditions tested and displayed stricter substrate and cleavage-site selection on pre-tRNA. Loss and re-expression of ELAC1 altered structured ncRNA abundance and small-RNA end profiles. These findings identify vtRNAs as direct ELAC1 substrates and support functional specialization of human ELAC paralogs, with ELAC2 favoring precise pre-tRNA maturation and ELAC1 exhibiting broader RNA substrate specificity.

title: Perturbation of the replication stress-ATR axis accelerates human erythroid differentiation but blocks terminal maturation
authors: Jauregui-Lozano, J.; Kremer, A.; Prummel, K. D.; Zaugg, J. B.
abstract: Replication stress (RS) can act as an input to differentiation: in erythroid and myeloid cells it is sufficient to accelerate commitment. Yet genotoxic chemotherapy, which imposes replication stress on the bone marrow can cause anemia; a frequent dose-limiting toxicity whose deficit of mature red cells is often attributed to progenitor depletion rather than to any effect on differentiation itself. Here, we ask how RS-induced accelerated commitment gives rise to impaired red cell output, using in vitro erythroid differentiation of cord-blood CD34+ progenitors perturbed with clinically relevant chemotherapy agents. We find that treated erythroblasts differentiate faster than controls but fail to mature, measured by lack of enucleated cells. Inhibition of ATR, but not ATM or DNA-PK, reproduces this phenotype. Mechanistically, single-cell profiling of drug-treated cells shows convergence on a transcriptional program, marked by loss of MYB and MYC activity. Treated cultures also accumulate aberrant late erythroblasts depleted for globin and heme programs and enriched for p53 and proteotoxic stress signatures. Together, these results propose that defective maturation is an alternative mechanism for chemotherapy-induced anemia, in addition to depletion of progenitors.
